If
$$\sum_{k=1}^{31}\left({ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{k}\right)\left({ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{k-1}\right)-\sum_{k=1}^{30}\left({ }^{30} \mathrm{C}_{k}\right)\left({ }^{30} \mathrm{C}_{k-1}\right)=\frac{\alpha(60!)}{(30!)(31!)},$$
Where $\alpha \in \mathrm{R}$, then the value of $16 \alpha$ is equal to

options.D:
1855

Official Ans. by NTA (A)
Ans. (A)
Sol.
$$\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{\mathrm{R}=1}^{31}{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{R}} \cdot{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{R}-1} \\
={ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{1} \cdot{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{0}+{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{2} \cdot{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{1}+\ldots+{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{31} \cdot{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{30} \\
={ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{0} \cdot{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{30}+{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{1} \cdot{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{29}+\ldots+{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{30} \cdot{ }^{31} \mathrm{C}_{0} \\
={ }^{62} \mathrm{C}_{30} \cdot
\end{array}$$

Similarly
$$\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{\mathrm{R}=1}^{30}\left({ }^{30} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{R}} \cdot{ }^{30} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{R}-1}\right)={ }^{60} \mathrm{C}_{29} \\
{ }^{62} \mathrm{C}_{30}-{ }^{60} \mathrm{C}_{29}=\frac{62!}{30!32!}-\frac{60!}{29!31!} \\
=\frac{60!}{29!31!}\left\{\frac{62 \cdot 61}{30 \cdot 32}-1\right\} \\
=\frac{60!}{30!31!}\left(\frac{2822}{32}\right) \\
\therefore 16 \alpha=16 \times \frac{2822}{32}=1411
\end{array}$$

Let a function $\mathrm{f}: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be defined by
$$f(n)=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
2 n, & n=2,4,6,8, \ldots . \\
n-1, & n=3,7,11,15, \ldots . . \\
\frac{n+1}{2}, & n=1,5,9,13, \ldots .
\end{array}\right.$$
then, f is

options.D:
one-one and onto

Official Ans. by NTA (D)
Ans. (D)

Sol. $\quad \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})=\left\{\begin{array}{ccc}4 \mathrm{R} & ; & \mathrm{n}=2 \mathrm{R} \\ 4 \mathrm{R}-2 & ; & \mathrm{n}=4 \mathrm{R}-1 \\ 2 \mathrm{R}-1 & ; & \mathrm{n}=4 \mathrm{R}-3\end{array}\right.$
$(\mathrm{R} \in \mathrm{N})$
Note that for any element, it will fall into exactly. one of these sets.
$$\begin{array}{l}
\{\mathrm{y}: \mathrm{y}=4 \mathrm{R} ; \mathrm{y} \in \mathrm{~N}\} \\
\{\mathrm{y}: \mathrm{y}=4 \mathrm{R}-2 ; \mathrm{y} \in \mathrm{~N}\} \\
\{\mathrm{y}: \mathrm{y}=2 \mathrm{R}-1 ; \mathrm{y} \in \mathrm{~N}\}
\end{array}$$

Corresponding to that y , we will get exactly one value of n.
Thus, f is one - one \& onto.

questions.text:
If the system of linear equations
$$\begin{array}{l}
2 x+3 y-z=-2 \\
x+y+z=4 \\
x-y+|\lambda| z=4 \lambda-4
\end{array}$$
where $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, has no solution, then

options.D:
$\lambda^{2}=1$

Official Ans. by NTA (B)
Ans. (B)
Sol. $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & |\lambda|\end{array}\right|=0$
$$\Rightarrow|\lambda|=7 \Rightarrow \lambda= \pm 7$$

System :
$$\begin{array}{l}
2 x+3 y-z=-2 \\
x+y+z=4 \\
x-y+|\lambda| z=4 \lambda-4
\end{array}$$

Eliminating y from equal (2) \& (3) we get
$$\begin{array}{l}
x+4 z=14 \\
(3)+(4) \Rightarrow x+\left(\frac{|\lambda|+1}{2}\right) z=2 \lambda
\end{array}$$

Clearly for $\lambda=-7$, system is inconsistent.

questions.text: Let A be a matrix of order $3 \times 3$ and $\operatorname{det}(\mathrm{A})=2$. Then $\operatorname{det}\left(\operatorname{det}(\mathrm{A}) \operatorname{adj}\left(5 \operatorname{adj}\left(\mathrm{~A}^{3}\right)\right)\right)$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$ .

options.D:
$256 \times 10^{11}$

Official Ans. by NTA (A)
Ans. (A)
Sol. |(det (A)) adj (5 adj (A))|
$$\begin{array}{l}
=\left|2 \operatorname{adj}\left(5 \operatorname{adj}\left(\mathrm{~A}^{3}\right)\right)\right| \\
=2^{3} \mid \operatorname{adj}\left(5 \operatorname{adj}\left(\mathrm{~A}^{3}\right)| |\right. \\
=2^{3} \cdot\left|5 \operatorname{adj}\left(\mathrm{~A}^{3}\right)\right|^{2} \\
=2^{3}\left(5^{3} \cdot\left|\operatorname{adj}\left(\mathrm{~A}^{3}\right)\right|\right)^{2} \\
=2^{3} \cdot 5^{6} \cdot\left|\operatorname{adj} \mathrm{~A}^{3}\right|^{2} \\
=2^{3} \cdot 5^{6}\left(\left(|\mathrm{~A}|^{3}\right)^{2}\right)^{2} \\
=2^{3} \cdot 5^{6} \cdot 2^{12}=2^{15} \times 5^{6} \\
\quad=2^{9} \times 10^{6} \\
\quad=512 \times 10^{6}
\end{array}$$

questions.text: The total number of 5-digit numbers, formed by using the digits 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 without repetition, which are multiple of 6 , is

options.D:
72

Official Ans. by NTA (D)
Ans. (D)
Sol. To make a no. divisible by 3 we can use the digits 1,2,5,6,7 or 1,2,3,5,7.

Using 1,2,5,6,7, number of even numbers is
$$=4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 \times 2=48$$

Using 1,2,3,5,7, number of even numbers is
$$=4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 \times 1=24$$

Required answer is 72.

questions.text: Let $\mathrm{A}_{1}, \mathrm{~A}_{2}, \mathrm{~A}_{3}$, $\_\_\_\_$ be an increasing geometric progression of positive real numbers. If $\mathrm{A}_{1} \mathrm{~A}_{3} \mathrm{~A}_{5} \mathrm{~A}_{7}=\frac{1}{1296}$ and $\mathrm{A}_{2}+\mathrm{A}_{4}=\frac{7}{36}$, then, the value of $\mathrm{A}_{6}+\mathrm{A}_{8}+\mathrm{A}_{10}$ is equal to

options.D:
47

Official Ans. by NTA (C)
Ans. (C)

Sol. $\quad \mathrm{A}_{1} \cdot \mathrm{~A}_{3} \cdot \mathrm{~A}_{5} \cdot \mathrm{~A}_{7}=\frac{1}{1296}$
$$\begin{array}{l}
\left(A_{4}\right)^{4}=\frac{1}{1296} \\
A_{4}=\frac{1}{6} \\
A_{2}+A_{4}=\frac{7}{36} \\
A_{2}=\frac{1}{36} \\
A_{6}=1 \\
A_{8}=6 \\
A_{10}=36 \\
A_{6}+A_{8}+A_{10}=43
\end{array}$$

questions.text:
Let $\mathrm{f}: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be defined as
$$f(x)=\left[\begin{array}{ll}
{\left[e^{x}\right],} & x<0 \\
a e^{x}+[x-1], & 0 \leq x<1 \\
b+[\sin (\pi x)], & 1 \leq x<2 \\
{\left[e^{-x}\right]-c,} & x \geq 2
\end{array}\right.$$
where $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $[\mathrm{t}]$ denotes greatest integer less than or equal to t. Then, which of the following statements is true ?

options.A: There exists $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c} \in \mathbb{R}$ such that f is continuous of $\mathbb{R}$.
options.B: If f is discontinuous at exactly one point, then $\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}+\mathrm{c}=1$.
options.C: If f is discontinuous at exactly one point, then $\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}+\mathrm{c} \neq 1$.
options.D:
f is discontinuous at atleast two points, for any values of a, b and c.

Official Ans. by NTA (C)
Ans. (C)
Sol. $\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ is discontinuous at $\mathrm{x}=1$
For continuous at $\mathrm{x}=0 ; \mathrm{a}=1$
For continuous at $\mathrm{x}=2 ; \mathrm{b}+\mathrm{c}=1$
$$a+b+c=2$$
